headline: Levers are force multipliers—trading distance for power to move the immovable
universal_truth: Leverage exists everywhere; small inputs can create large outputs when positioned correctly
fun_facts: Archimedes said: 'Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I shall move the world'
Your arm is a lever—your elbow is the fulcrum, muscles apply force, and your hand moves objects
A crowbar can multiply your force by 10 times or more
discussion_questions: Where do you see levers in everyday life?
What's the trade-off when using a lever?
Where in life can you apply 'leverage' to multiply your efforts?

hook.script: A boulder weighs a ton. You weigh much less. Yet with a long enough lever, you could lift that boulder with one hand. Levers are force multipliers—simple machines that let weak humans move heavy worlds.

cliff.script: If levers multiply force, do they create energy from nothing? That would violate physics. So what's the trade-off? Where does the extra force come from?

options.text: Levers trade distance for force—you push farther to lift something a shorter distance
options.response: Yes. No free lunch—you push through a longer arc to move the load a shorter distance. Same energy, different arrangement.

options.text: Levers store energy in the fulcrum and release it on the other side
options.response: The fulcrum enables the trade-off, but the real exchange is distance for force...

fact1.title: The Trade-Off
fact1.script: Levers don't create force—they redistribute it. Push down one meter to lift something 10 centimeters, and you've multiplied your force by 10. You do the same total work, just spread differently. Physics always balances.

fact2.title: Your Body's Levers
fact2.script: Your skeleton is full of levers. Your forearm is a lever—elbow as fulcrum, bicep providing force, hand doing work. Your jaw is a lever. Even your skull pivots on your spine as a lever. You're a machine made of levers.

fact3.title: Three Classes
fact3.script: Levers come in three classes based on where the fulcrum, effort, and load sit. Seesaws, wheelbarrows, and fishing rods are all levers—but each places these elements differently. Same principle, many configurations.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Leverage exists everywhere. In physics and in life, small inputs can create large outputs when positioned correctly. Find the fulcrum, apply force at the right point, and move the immovable.

outro.script: That's Day 113. Tomorrow, we'll discover how to lift heavy things easily—pulleys. Until then, notice the levers around you, including the ones in your own body.

growTrack.title: Life Leverage - Find Your Fulcrum
growTrack.learning_objective: Apply the concept of leverage to life situations
growTrack.activity: Where in your life could you apply leverage—small inputs creating large outputs? A skill that opens many doors? A relationship that multiplies opportunities? Identify one area where you could find better leverage.
